artifacts.summary: All six plan phases complete: refined noise-tolerant three-pattern binder/hat-abstraction exemption reaches zero on both false-positive fixtures, leaves the true-positive and both MIXED fixtures' counts exactly unchanged, closes the research's stated true-positive verification gap via a fresh primary-tier reconversion (rejected at 9 hits, identical under old and new exemption), and records the MIXED-document decision and pymupdf4llm-fragmentation lesson for future implementers.

completion_data.completion_summary: Widened sentence_boundary_glue_count()'s binder exemption to stop rejecting real higher-order-logic/lambda-notation papers (goodman_2024, bacon_a_case both reach 0), while leaving the true-positive fixture (verified via a fresh pymupdf4llm reconversion: 9 hits, unchanged from the pre-fix count) and both MIXED fixtures (hott_book_2013=11, ahrens_north=21, unchanged) correctly rejected. Added a regression harness, five new self-test fixtures, and a domain-context note on pymupdf4llm's extraction-fragmentation and self-interference hazards.

memory_candidates.content: When widening a regex exemption applied via strip-then-count (re.sub matched spans, then re.findall on what remains), an unanchored substitution pattern that starts with a common character class (e.g. [a-z]) and only fails after scanning forward for a rare terminating glyph is expensive at document scale under Python's backtracking re engine — measured ~19x slowdown on a 1.28MB document versus the narrow pattern it replaced. Bounding the pattern's internal lazy quantifier alone is insufficient (still ~10-15x). The effective fix is algorithmic: scan forward from each occurrence of the RARE anchor character instead (via re.finditer on that single character), and test only a small bounded window immediately preceding each occurrence with an end-anchored compiled pattern. This restores runtime to within ~10% of baseline. Applies to any regex-based text-corruption/exemption check run over whole-document content, not just this specific case.

When building a regression harness that concatenates multiple chunked source files (e.g. chunk_0001.md, chunk_0002.md, ...) to feed a text-analysis function whose output depends on character adjacency (e.g. counting [a-z]\.[A-Z] boundary transitions), raw string concatenation of chunks can manufacture or suppress matches at chunk seams: the last character of one chunk glues directly onto the first character of the next. This was measured directly: two of five fixtures' counts were wrong by 2-15x under raw concatenation versus joining chunks with a blank-line separator ("\n\n".join). Always join chunked source files with an explicit separator when the downstream analysis is adjacency-sensitive, and verify the harness reproduces any known/reported baseline numbers before trusting it.
